questions.model_answer:
a) CSF pleocytosis - Polio: Yes (with only minimally elevated protein). GBS: No (albuminocytologic dissociation: elevated protein with absent or minimal pleocytosis).
Symmetrical weakness - Polio: No (asymmetrical distribution is the most characteristic feature; proximal > distal, legs > arms). GBS: Yes (symmetrical, bilateral ascending paralysis).
Loss of sensation - Polio: No (sensory loss is very rare; dorsal root ganglia are involved pathologically but without sensory deficit, and sensory loss should suggest another diagnosis). GBS: Yes.

cohort_answer.text: Pleocytosis of CSF: Polio=Yes (initially PMN with shift to lymphocytosis); GBS=No (normal WBC but elevated protein = albuminocytologic dissociation). Symmetrical weakness: Polio=No (asymmetric); GBS=Yes. Loss of sensation: Polio=No; GBS=Yes.

questions.model_answer:
a) The anterior horns of the spinal cord (gray matter) - poliovirus destroys the motor (anterior horn) neurons, with inflammatory lesions of PMNs, lymphocytes and macrophages distributed through the anterior horn gray matter.
b) (1) Cranial nerve IX (glossopharyngeal). (2) Cranial nerve X (vagus) - producing pharyngeal paralysis with pooling of secretions, dysphagia and nasal speech.

cohort_answer.text: Anatomical structure: Anterior horn cells. Cranial nerves: CN9, CN10 (dysphagia, dysarthria).

cohort_answer.text: Table: CSF Pleocytosis - Polio: High cells and protein; GBS: Normal cells (Typically), High protein. Symmetric Weakness - Polio: Asymmetric proximal to distal and usually single extremity and affects lower limbs; GBS: Symmetric ascending. Loss of Sensation - Polio: No (very rare except severe cases); GBS: Yes. Important to differentiate GBS from Poliomyelitis as treatment can be given for GBS. Other viral causes of AFP: Non-polio enteroviruses (enterovirus D68, enterovirus A71); WNV; Japanese encephalitis virus; Polio; Tick-borne encephalitis virus; St. Louis encephalitis; also coxsackie A7, echovirus, flavivirus, Zika, rabies, HIV, HTLV-1. Anatomical structure: Viremic phase seeds to CNS or CNS axonal transport and replication occurs in the anterior horn cells of spine. Cranial nerves: Glossopharyngeal (IX), X (vagus).

questions.question: Poliomyelitis versus Guillain-Barre syndrome.

parts.text: CSF findings.
Fever?
Neurological syndrome in detail.
Speed of progression.

parts_raw.text: A) CSF findings
B) fever?
C) Neurological syndrome in detail
D) Speed of progression

questions.model_answer:
a) Polio: pleocytosis with a minimally elevated protein and normal glucose - indistinguishable from other viral aseptic meningitides; poliovirus is rarely isolated from CSF. GBS: elevated protein with absent or minimal pleocytosis (albuminocytologic dissociation).
b) Polio: yes - fever accompanies both the minor and the major illness, and progression of paralysis stops when the patient becomes afebrile. GBS: no.
c) Polio: preceded by meningitic features (fever, headache, vomiting, neck stiffness) plus severe myalgia, hyperesthesia/paresthesia, spasm and fasciculation for 1-2 days; then acute flaccid weakness ranging from one muscle to quadriplegia; characteristically asymmetrical, proximal > distal, legs > arms; deep tendon reflexes initially hyperactive then absent; sensation spared; bladder paralysis in ~25% of adults; bulbar involvement in 5%-35% of paralytic cases (CN IX/X, dysphagia, nasal speech, pooled secretions); respiratory failure from diaphragm/intercostal paralysis, airway obstruction or medullary centre involvement. GBS: symmetrical, bilateral, ascending flaccid paralysis with loss of sensation and areflexia.
d) Polio: incubation 9-12 days to prodrome and 11-17 days to paralysis; paralysis extends over 2-3 days, occasionally up to 1 week, and stops with defervescence. GBS: progression over 1-2 weeks.

cohort_answer.text:
A) Polio: Pleocytosis, protein elevation, normal glucose, uncommon to isolate. Acute polio: pleocytosis + minimally elevated protein (CSF abnormalities not distinguishable from other viral aseptic meningitis). GBS: usually NO pleocytosis (protein elevated - albumin-cytologic dissociation); when pleocytosis occurs, 50% in first week and mostly in HIV+ patients; absent or minimal pleocytosis with elevated protein.

B) Polio: yes. GBS: no.

C) Polio: Weakness varies from one muscle to quadriplegia/respiratory failure; proximal>distal, legs>arms; worsens over 2-3 days (sometimes up to a week); reduced tone, typically asymmetric; reflexes decreased/absent; bulbar involvement in 5-35% (dysphagia, dysarthria, difficulty handling secretions); sensory almost always normal; sometimes encephalitis (usually infancy); respiratory insufficiency may occur. GBS: Progressive, mostly symmetric muscle weakness, progresses over 2 weeks; distal>>proximal; reflexes absent/depressed; severe respiratory muscle weakness needing ventilatory support in 30%; major complications (pneumonia, sepsis, PE, GI bleed) in 60% of intubated patients; dysautonomia in 70%; 20% remain unable to walk at 6 months in severe cases.

D) Polio: Incubation period 9-12 days; onset of paralysis 11-17 days; weakness progresses over 2-3 days. GBS: unclear antecedent period; symptoms usually progress over 2-4 weeks (UTD); plateau can occur between 12 hours and 28 days.

parts.text: Fill in the table comparing polio and Guillain-Barre syndrome across: causative, motor/sensory, neuron involved, weakness nature, nerve conduction, tendon reflex, CSF pleocytosis, fever, neurological syndrome, speed of progression.

parts_raw.text: Fill in the table comparing Polio and GBS across: Causative, Motor/sensory, Neuron involved, Weakness nature, Nerve conduction, Tendon Reflex, CSF pleocytosis, Fever, Neuro syndrome, Speed of progression.

questions.model_answer:
a) Causative - Polio: poliovirus (enterovirus, 3 serotypes; wild-type, vaccine-related or vaccine-derived); GBS: post-infectious autoimmune.
Motor/sensory - Polio: motor (and autonomic) only; GBS: motor and sensory.
Neuron involved - Polio: anterior horn motor neuron of the spinal cord and motor nuclei of pons/medulla; GBS: peripheral nerve/root.
Weakness nature - Polio: asymmetrical flaccid, proximal > distal, legs > arms; GBS: symmetrical ascending.
Nerve conduction - Polio: normal (anterior horn cell disease); GBS: slowed or absent (demyelinating).
Tendon reflex - Polio: initially hyperactive, then absent; GBS: absent/depressed.
CSF pleocytosis - Polio: yes, with minimally elevated protein; GBS: no - albuminocytologic dissociation.
Fever - Polio: yes; GBS: no.
Neurological syndrome - Polio: meningitic prodrome, myalgia, asymmetrical flaccid paralysis with preserved sensation, bulbar involvement in 5%-35% (CN IX/X), respiratory failure; GBS: symmetrical bilateral ascending paralysis with sensory loss.
Speed of progression - Polio: paralysis extends over 2-3 days (occasionally up to 1 week) and stops with defervescence; GBS: progresses over 1-2 weeks.
questions.beyond_mandell: Nerve conduction findings and the autoimmune/post-infectious pathogenesis of GBS are not in this Mandell chapter (standard neurology teaching: polio = normal conduction with denervation on EMG; GBS = demyelinating slowing/conduction block).
questions.cohort_conflict: Cohort answer calls polio weakness "descending within the limb muscles"; Mandell p. 2222 describes it simply as asymmetrical with proximal muscles more involved than distal.

cohort_answer.text:
Causative | Polio virus | Autoimmune, may be triggered by infection
Motor/sensory | Motor | Both
Neuron involved | Anterior horn of spinal cord | Peripheral neurons
Weakness nature | Asymmetrical, descending within the limb muscles | Symmetrical and ascending
Nerve conduction | normal | slow/absent
Tendon Reflex | absent | absent
CSF pleocytosis | Yes - initially PMNs then lymphocytic | No
Fever | Yes | No
Neuro syndrome | Prox -> distal, asymmetric, bulbar involvement 5-35%, normal sensory | Distal -> proximal, reflexes absent, symmetric, severe resp distress req vent in 30%
Speed of progression | 2-3 days | 2-4 weeks

questions.question: Poliovirus.

parts.text: 2 clinical characteristics.
Describe post-polio syndrome.

parts_raw.text: A. 2 clinical characteristics
B. describe post-polio syndrome

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Asymptomatic/inapparent infection in at least 95%, recognized only by virus isolation from feces or oropharynx or an antibody rise. (2) Abortive poliomyelitis in 4%-8%: 2-3 days of fever with headache, sore throat, listlessness, anorexia, vomiting or abdominal pain and a normal neurological examination. (Others: nonparalytic poliomyelitis - aseptic meningitis; spinal paralytic poliomyelitis in ~0.1%, asymmetrical flaccid paralysis with preserved sensation; bulbar poliomyelitis in 5%-35% of paralytic cases; polioencephalitis in infants.)
b) A new onset of muscle weakness, pain, atrophy and fatigue years after partial or full recovery from paralytic poliomyelitis. Typically the same muscles as the original illness, though previously unaffected limbs may be involved. Onset is gradual and progression slow; patients are seldom severely disabled, but it is dangerous in those with respiratory dysfunction or dysphagia. It affects 20%-85% of previously paralyzed patients, with a mean interval of 36 years from the acute illness. The cause is unknown; the leading theory is physiologic attrition of motor units already depleted by the original infection.

cohort_answer.text:
A: Asymptomatic: At least 95% of infections are asymptomatic or unapparent and can be recognized only by the isolation of poliovirus from feces or oropharynx or by a rise in antibody titer. Abortive poliomyelitis: occurs in 4-8% of infections, 2-3 day period of fever, headache, sore throat, listlessness, anorexia, vomiting, or abdominal pain; neurologic exam normal. Nonparalytic poliomyelitis: differs from abortive poliomyelitis by presence of signs of meningeal irritation; identical to meningitis caused by other enteroviruses. Spinal paralytic poliomyelitis: 0.1% of polio infections; biphasic course with minor and major illnesses in ~1/3 of children with paralytic poliomyelitis. Bulbar paralytic poliomyelitis: paralysis of muscle groups innervated by cranial nerves, especially soft palate and pharynx - dysphagia, nasal speech, sometimes dyspnea; if CN IX and X involved, pharyngeal paralysis with pooling of secretions. Polioencephalitis: uncommon, occurs primarily in infants - confusion, disturbances of consciousness, seizures, spastic paralysis

B: After full recovery from paralytic polio, new onset of progressive muscle weakness, pain, atrophy, fatigue up to 36 years later. Generally same muscle groups involved. Gradual onset. Affects 20-85% of previously paralyzed patients. Cause unknown

parts_raw.text: A. What is most likely diagnosis and why?
B) One investigation to help confirm diagnosis?
C) 4 infectious causes of acute flaccid paralysis?
D) Explain the pathophysiology of GBS in this patient

questions.model_answer:
a) Guillain-Barre syndrome following Campylobacter jejuni enteritis. The antecedent diarrheal illness fits the recognized C. jejuni-GBS association (GBS usually 2-3 weeks post-infection; C. jejuni is the leading recognized antecedent). Argues against poliomyelitis: he is not from/exposed to a polio-endemic area, has no sick contacts, and sensory involvement with ascending weakness favours GBS over the pure motor picture of polio (oral polio vaccine in the child is a red herring).
b) Lumbar puncture showing albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF (raised protein with normal cell count); nerve conduction studies/EMG are also confirmatory.
c) (1) Poliovirus (poliomyelitis) (2) Non-polio enteroviruses (e.g., enterovirus D68, EV71) (3) West Nile virus (4) Corynebacterium diphtheriae (diphtheritic neuropathy). [C. jejuni-associated GBS is itself an additional infection-related cause.]
d) Molecular mimicry: C. jejuni LPS/lipooligosaccharide bears sialylated structures resembling human peripheral-nerve gangliosides (GM1, GD1a, GD3, GT1a). Cross-reactive autoantibodies generated against the organism attack these ganglioside epitopes on peripheral nerves; O:19 and certain capsular genotypes are over-represented in GBS.
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts b) and c) are not detailed in this Mandell chapter; CSF albuminocytologic dissociation/NCS and the list of infectious AFP causes (polio, enteroviruses, WNV, diphtheria) rest on standard neurology/CDC AFP knowledge.

cohort_answer.text:
A) Guillain-Barre syndrome secondary to Campylobacter gastroenteritis. No indication that the patient himself acquired a vector of a polio-like illness, nor were there sick contacts; no indication he was in an endemic region for polio (Afghanistan, Pakistan); sensory involvement would strongly indicate GBS vs polio.

B) CSF for albumin-cytologic dissociation. (Discussion: CSF classical findings seen in only 50% of patients; serial nerve conduction studies and EMG may be preferred. Albuminocytologic dissociation present in 50-66% of GBS patients in first week, ≥75% by third week; normal CSF protein found in 1/3-1/2 of patients tested earlier than 1 week and does not exclude GBS. NCS/EMG valuable for confirming diagnosis, prognosis, and classifying GBS as demyelinating vs axonal.)

C) WNV, Poliomyelitis, non-polio enteroviruses, Diphtheria.

D) Molecular mimicry - Campylobacter contains ganglioside-like epitopes in the lipopolysaccharide moiety that elicit autoantibodies reacting with peripheral nerve targets. Close resemblance of these sialylated structures to human gangliosides (GM1, GD1a, GD3, GT1a) and their presence in strains isolated from GBS patients supports a role in pathogenesis. Campylobacter outer membranes contain lipopolysaccharides (O-antigen) with endotoxic activity; O-antigens possess sialic acid-containing structures recognized by host immune cells with sialoadhesins, similar to human gangliosides.
